kurals.tamil:
எண்பதத்தால் எய்தல் எளிதென்ப யார்மாட்டும்
பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Enpadhaththaal eydhal elidhenpa yaarmaattum
panputaimai ennum vazhakku.
kurals.meaning: People say that for someone who is easy for anyone to approach, the noble way called courtesy comes easily.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a class helper whose door is always open, who smiles at every kid, big or small, and listens. Being kind and polite is easy for that helper because they already let everyone come close. Valluvar says good manners grow out of being easy to reach.
kurals.university: The chapter on panbudaimai (பண்புடைமை, 'possession of refined character, courtesy') opens with a practical claim: the path is easy for the one who has en-padham (எண்பதம்), 'easy access', the quality of being approachable (எளிய செவ்வி) to everyone, yaar-maattum (யார்மாட்டும், 'towards whomsoever'). Puliyur Kesikan on thirukkural.net and Mu. Varadarasanar on ytamizh both gloss en-padham as எளிய செவ்வி, availability to all comers, and vazhakku (வழக்கு) as the established good path or usage; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the claim is reported, 'say the learned' (நூலோர் கூறுவர்), reflecting the verb enpa (என்ப, 'they say'). Sivayogi Sivakumar's reading of en as 'numbers' (speaking in words as plain as numerals) is an idiosyncratic minority interpretation not shared by the classical glosses. Pope renders the couplet 'Who easy access give to every man, they say, / Of kindly courtesy will learn with ease the way', and the same accessibility motif appears in the earlier kural 386 on the king who is kaatchikku eliyan (easy of audience). Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Saanraanmai (ch. 99), the chapter turns from the inner perfection of the noble to its outward social face. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not envious but is a kind friend to all living entities, who does not think himself a proprietor and is free from false ego, who is equal in both happiness and distress, who is tolerant, always satisfied, self-controlled, and engaged in devotional service with determination, his mind and intelligence fixed on Me – such a devotee of Mine is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists the marks of the beloved devotee, beginning with being free of envy and a kindly friend (maitraḥ karuṇaḥ) to every living being.
hinduism.tie_back: Being a friend to all without exception is the same open, easy-to-reach disposition the Kural calls the easy road to courtesy.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 12.13–14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; shares the universal friendliness theme but frames it as devotion rather than social approachability.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers not to hold themselves aloof but to come down to and associate with ordinary and lowly people.
christianity.tie_back: Refusing to stand on dignity and staying reachable by the lowly is exactly the 'easy access to all' that the Kural sets as the gateway to courtesy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a strong match on approachability across rank, though it speaks of humility rather than naming courtesy.

islam.quote_or_event: “Any of the female slaves of Medina could take hold of the hand of Allah's Messenger (ﷺ) and take him wherever she wished.”
islam.explanation: Anas reports that the Prophet was so approachable that even the humblest slave-girl of Medina could lead him by the hand to attend to her need.
islam.tie_back: This is a living picture of en-padham, the easy accessibility to anyone that the Kural says makes courtesy come naturally.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6072, Book of Good Manners (Al-Adab), chapter on pride and arrogance
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; an unusually close illustration of accessibility to all, placed in the book of manners.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shammai used to say: make your [study of the] Torah a fixed practice; speak little, but do much; and receive all men with a pleasant countenance.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah's ethical tractate teaches that every person, without distinction, should be greeted warmly and graciously.
judaism.tie_back: Receiving all men pleasantly is the open-door manner that, in the Kural, makes the path of courtesy easy.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:15 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a near one-to-one match on welcoming everyone, though it does not frame this as the means to a larger virtue.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Who is hospitable, and friendly, / Liberal and unselfish, / A guide, an instructor, a leader, / Such a one to honor may attain.”
buddhism.explanation: In the householder's code the Buddha praises the hospitable and friendly person as one who rises to honour.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes friendliness toward all the ground on which a person's refined standing is built.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good thematic match on friendliness and hospitality, though the reward named is honour rather than courtesy itself.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's lecture on discipline (vinaya) contrasts rough, ill-behaved conduct with polite, accommodating manners that win over even a difficult person.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain text, like the Kural, treats easy, pleasant bearing toward others as what makes good conduct succeed.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable fit on politeness, though the setting is a monastic pupil and teacher rather than accessibility to all.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid's tale, Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as mortals, are turned away from a thousand doors until the poor old couple Baucis and Philemon welcome them, and they alone are rewarded when the inhospitable valley is flooded.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story celebrates the humble couple whose door and hearth were open to unknown strangers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their openness to whoever came is the same easy accessibility that the Kural treats as the doorway to true courtesy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth; it illustrates hospitality to strangers rather than the general social approachability the Kural describes.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For he will behave so alike towards those he knows and those he does not know, towards intimates and those who are not so, except that in each of these cases he will behave as is befitting.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the nameless social virtue between obsequiousness and churlishness, by which a man is pleasant in the right way toward everyone he meets.
philosophy.tie_back: Treating known and unknown alike with fitting pleasantness is Aristotle's version of the Kural's courtesy toward 'whomsoever'.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.6 (tr. W. D. Ross, Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a strong conceptual match for courtesy extended to all, though Aristotle does not speak of accessibility as its cause.

kurals.tamil:
அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல் இவ்விரண்டும்
பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Anputaimai aandra kutippiraththal ivvirantum
panputaimai ennum vazhakku.
kurals.meaning: Loving kindness toward others and birth into a worthy family: these two together make up the way called courtesy.
kurals.elementary: Think of a kind heart as the seed and a good home as the garden it grows in. When a child has both a loving heart and a family that teaches good ways, gentle manners bloom. Valluvar says courtesy needs both.
kurals.university: The second couplet names the two roots of panbudaimai: anbudaimai (அன்புடைமை, 'possession of love', the title of chapter 8) and aandra kudip-piraththal (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல், 'being born in an eminent, accomplished family'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take aandra kudi as a high or noble family, while Solomon Pappaiah reinterprets it as a family that 'lives in harmony with the world' (உலகத்தோடு ஒத்து வாழும் குடும்பம்), softening the hereditary emphasis; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as living a birth worth reflecting on. Pope's 'Benevolence and high born dignity, / These two are beaten paths of courtesy' preserves vazhakku (வழக்கு) as a 'beaten path' or established usage. The kural links this chapter back to Kudimai (ch. 96, 'Nobility of family'), which places good family upbringing at the base of character; modern readers often stress that the second element is about formation and tradition rather than caste rank. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The unsuccessful yogī, after many, many years of enjoyment on the planets of the pious living entities, is born into a family of righteous people, or into a family of rich aristocracy.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna assures Arjuna that one whose spiritual effort was cut short is reborn into a righteous or noble household, where good formation can resume.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita, like the Kural, treats birth into a worthy family as a real support for refined character.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.41 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it values good birth as a fruit of merit, but says nothing about loving kindness or courtesy as such.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up, Doth not behave itself unseemly, seeketh not her own, is not easily provoked, thinketh no evil;”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes love as patient and kind and as the thing that keeps a person from behaving unseemly, that is, discourteously.
christianity.tie_back: This joins the Kural's first root, love, directly to courteous behaviour, though it omits the role of family.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong on love producing seemly conduct, but silent on the Kural's second element of good birth.

islam.quote_or_event: “You see that the people are of different natures. Those who were the best in the pre-lslamic period, are also the best in Islam if they comprehend religious knowledge.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet compares people to mines of differing quality, saying the noble-natured before Islam remain the best within it when they gain understanding.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats inherited good nature as a foundation that, joined with right understanding, yields excellence of character.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 3493, 3494 (Book of Virtues and Merits)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a real parallel on inherited nobility, though the hadith's second ingredient is religious understanding rather than love.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the people of Israel are known by three family traits, being merciful, being bashful or modest, and performing acts of kindness, and that whoever has these traits is fit to join the people.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis define belonging to the people by inherited moral traits of compassion, modesty and kindness rather than by bloodline alone.
judaism.tie_back: It fuses the Kural's two roots, a kindly heart and the character of a worthy lineage, into one definition of a refined people.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of a well-known passage and not re-verified this session, so not quoted; a strong thematic fit joining kindness and lineage.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vasala Sutta the Buddha tells the brahmin Aggika Bharadvaja that one does not become an outcast or a brahmin by birth, but by one's deeds.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha rejects birth as the measure of worth and locates nobility entirely in conduct.
buddhism.tie_back: This stands in tension with the Kural's second root, offering a contrast: for the Buddha, kindness and conduct alone make the noble person.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; included as an honest contrast, since the sutta denies the value of birth that the Kural affirms.

jainism.quote_or_event: “By one's actions one becomes a Brâhmana, or a Kshattriya, or a Vaisya, or a Sûdra.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Gayaghosha tells a sacrificing priest that a person's station is made by deeds, not by birth.
jainism.tie_back: Jainism, like Buddhism, would ground courtesy in conduct rather than lineage, which qualifies the Kural's appeal to good birth.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.33 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a partial contrast rather than a match, since it denies birth the role the Kural gives it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Telemachus and Pisistratus arrive at Sparta, Menelaus welcomes them before learning their names and remarks that their bearing shows they come of a line of sceptred kings, since base men could not have such sons.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Homer, gracious and noble bearing is read as the visible mark of good birth.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It reflects the Kural's assumption that a worthy family shows itself in refined manners.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not re-verified this session; it matches the good-birth element but not the element of love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle distinguishes being well-born (eugenes), the excellence of one's stock, from being noble in character (gennaios), noting that the well-born often degenerate and fail to live up to their ancestry.
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle grants that good birth is a real advantage but insists it must be matched by personal excellence.
philosophy.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural's pairing: lineage alone is insufficient unless joined to a kindly character.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not re-verified this session; a partial match on the role of birth, without Aristotle's mention of love.

kurals.tamil:
உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால் வெறுத்தக்க
பண்பொத்தல் ஒப்பதாம் ஒப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
Uruppoththal makkaloppu andraal veruththakka
panpoththal oppadhaam oppu.
kurals.meaning: Having the same body parts does not make people truly alike; real likeness is likeness in the good, agreeable qualities of character.
kurals.elementary: Two dolls can look exactly the same on the outside, but one might be stuffed with cotton and the other with sharp pins. People are like that too: having two eyes and two hands like someone does not make you like them. Being kind like them does.
kurals.university: Uruppu-oththal (உறுப்பொத்தல், 'sameness of limbs') is denied the status of makkal-oppu (மக்களொப்பு, 'likeness among humans'); true oppu is panb-oththal (பண்பொத்தல்), likeness in qualities. The crux is veruththakka (வெறுத்தக்க): Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as 'fit to be joined' (பொருந்தத்தக்க), Solomon Pappaiah as qualities that unite heart with heart, and Pope as 'kindred quality' ('Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true'), reflecting the older commentarial reading of வெறு as 'to be close, to cohere'. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads it in the modern sense 'hateful', yielding 'likeness in shunning what deserves shunning', a minority interpretation. Kalaignar draws the strong conclusion that only those alike in good qualities deserve to be counted as human at all, which anticipates kural 997. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Pṛthā, in this world there are two kinds of created beings. One is called divine and the other demoniac. I have already explained to you at length the divine qualities. Now hear from Me of the demoniac.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna divides human beings not by appearance or birth but by whether they bear divine or demonic qualities.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it classes people by their qualities rather than their bodily sameness.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.6 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a reasonable match on classing people by qualities, though it does not contrast this with bodily likeness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.”
christianity.explanation: When Samuel is impressed by Eliab's looks, God tells him that the true measure of a person is the heart, not the body.
christianity.tie_back: This sets aside outward bodily form in favour of inner character, as the Kural does.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong match on body versus character, though it concerns divine judgement rather than human resemblance.

islam.quote_or_event: “Verily Allah does not look to your faces and your wealth but He looks to your heart and to your deeds.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that appearance and possessions count for nothing before God compared with the heart and actions.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, a person's real identity lies in qualities and deeds, not in the shape of the face or body.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 2564c (Book of Virtue, Enjoining Good Manners)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a close conceptual match, framed in terms of divine regard.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi said: don’t look at the container but at that which is in it: there is a new container full of old wine, and an old [container] in which there is not even new [wine].”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince warns that outward vessels deceive and that worth lies in what they hold.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's point is the same: the body is a container, and true likeness lies in the qualities within.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:20 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a vivid match on outer form versus inner content, though originally said of teachers' age.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vasettha Sutta the Buddha explains that grasses, insects, animals, fish and birds show distinct marks of species by birth, but among human beings there are no such distinguishing bodily marks; distinctions among humans are only by name, and a person is what his deeds make him.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha argues that human bodies are basically alike, so the real differences between people must lie in conduct.
buddhism.tie_back: This is close to the Kural's argument: bodily sameness is shared by all, and what truly distinguishes or unites people is their qualities.
buddhism.source: Vasettha Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.9 (also Majjhima Nikaya 98)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, as the online text could not be re-fetched this session; the argument structure closely parallels the Kural.

jainism.quote_or_event: “One does not become a Sramana by the tonsure, nor a Brâhmana by the sacred syllable ôm, nor a Muni by living in the woods, nor a Tâpasa by wearing (clothes of) Kusa-grass and bark. One becomes a Sramana by equanimity, a Brâhmana by chastity, a Muni by knowledge, and a Tâpasa by penance.”
jainism.explanation: Gayaghosha teaches that outward marks such as a shaven head or bark clothing do not make a monk or sage; only the inner qualities do.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it rejects outward resemblance as the measure of a person and locates true likeness in character.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.31–32 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong fit on outer marks versus inner qualities, though applied to religious roles rather than humanity as such.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Circe turns Odysseus' companions into swine, they take on the heads, voices and bristles of pigs, yet their minds remain as before, and they weep in their sties.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer imagines bodies changed into beasts while the human mind stays intact.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The myth makes the Kural's point from the other side: what makes someone human is not the shape of the limbs but what is within.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not re-verified this session; an inverse illustration rather than a direct parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, as he went about, ‘I am looking for a man.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes the Cynic mocked the crowds of Athens by implying that among all the human bodies around him he could not find a true human being.
philosophy.tie_back: Diogenes dramatizes the Kural's claim that sharing the human form does not make one truly human.
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (tr. R. D. Hicks, via Wikisource)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Wikisource; a near one-to-one match on bodily humanity versus true humanity.

kurals.tamil:
நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த பயனுடையார்
பண்புபா ராட்டும் உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nayanotu nandri purindha payanutaiyaar
panpupaa raattum ulaku.
kurals.meaning: The world praises the character of those who are useful to others because they love justice and do good.
kurals.elementary: When a kid is fair in games and also helps others when they fall, everyone on the playground says, 'She's so nice!' Valluvar says people love and praise those who are both fair and helpful.
kurals.university: The couplet pairs nayan (நயன், 'justice, equity, fairness') with nanri (நன்றி, 'beneficence, doing good'), and calls those who 'cherish' (purindha, புரிந்த) both payan-udaiyaar (பயனுடையார்), people who are of real use to others. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the pair as நீதியும் நன்மையும், Pappaiah as நீதியும் அறமும், and Pope's prose 'equity and charity' follows the same traditional line. The result is that ulagu (உலகு, 'the world', i.e. the discerning public) 'praises' (paaraattum, பாராட்டும்) their panbu. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes nayan as conduct that gives delight, a looser reading. The kural shows that courtesy in Valluvar is not mere politeness of speech but includes just and beneficial action. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Whatever action a great man performs, common men follow. And whatever standards he sets by exemplary acts, all the world pursues.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna that the conduct of an exemplary person becomes the standard the whole world follows.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it describes the world responding to the visible good conduct of the worthy, though as imitation rather than praise.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.21 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a partial match, since it speaks of being followed rather than of praise for justice and beneficence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his followers that their good deeds, seen by others, will lead people to give glory.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's world that praises the useful and good finds an echo here, though the glory is directed to God.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good match on good works seen and praised, with the praise redirected to God.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah orders justice and good conduct and giving to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an commands both justice ('adl) and excellent good conduct (ihsan) together.
islam.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's pairing of nayan and nanri, justice joined with beneficence.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close match on the justice-plus-goodness pairing, though it is a divine command rather than a statement about public praise.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let not mercy and truth forsake thee: bind them about thy neck; write them upon the table of thine heart: So shalt thou find favour and good understanding in the sight of God and man.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs promises that one who holds fast to kindness and faithfulness will win favour with both God and people.
judaism.tie_back: Kindness and truth winning the favour of men is close to the Kural's justice and goodness winning the world's praise.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong structural match of two virtues leading to public esteem.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “People hold dear him who embodies virtue and insight, who is principled, has realized the truth, and who himself does what he ought to be doing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that people cherish the one who is virtuous, principled and does his duty.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the world's affection and esteem follow genuine virtue in action.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 217 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a good match on being held dear for virtue, without the Kural's explicit pairing of justice and beneficence.

jainism.quote_or_event: “An intelligent man who has learned (the sacred texts) takes his duties upon himself, and he becomes renowned in the world; as the earth is the dwelling of all beings, so he will be a dwelling of all duties.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline says the conscientious disciple who shoulders his duties becomes famous and supports others as the earth supports all beings.
jainism.tie_back: Renown that comes from bearing duties for others is close to the Kural's praise for those who are useful through justice and goodness.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.45 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable fit on renown earned by dutiful usefulness, set in a monastic context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Disguised as a beggar, Odysseus tells Penelope that her fame reaches heaven like that of a blameless king who upholds justice, under whom the land bears fruit and the people prosper.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer links just rule and the flourishing it brings with wide renown.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's world praising those whose justice benefits others is reflected in this image of the just king's fame.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not re-verified this session; it shares the justice-brings-renown motif but in a royal setting.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that people's affection and esteem are won above all by kindness and generosity, and their confidence by a reputation for justice, so that justice joined with beneficence is the surest path to true glory.
philosophy.explanation: In his treatise on duties Cicero analyses how goodwill and glory are earned, naming beneficence and justice as the chief means.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero's analysis closely matches the Kural's claim that justice and doing good win the world's praise.
philosophy.source: Cicero, De Officiis II.9–11 and II.32–38
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not re-verified this session; the thematic correspondence is strong but section numbers are approximate.

kurals.tamil:
நகையுள்ளும் இன்னா திகழ்ச்சி பகையுள்ளும்
பண்புள பாடறிவார் மாட்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nakaiyullum innaa thikazhchchi pakaiyullum
panpula paadarivaar maattu.
kurals.meaning: Mocking someone hurts even when it is only a joke; so those who understand people keep their courtesy even toward enemies.
kurals.elementary: Calling someone a silly name 'just for fun' can still make them cry inside. Kids who really understand feelings don't do it, not even to a kid they're cross with. Valluvar says being polite even to someone you don't like is a sign of real wisdom.
kurals.university: The first line states a psychological fact: igazhchi (இகழ்ச்சி, 'contempt, ridicule') is innaa (இன்னா, 'painful') even within nagai (நகை, 'laughter, jest'). The second draws the ethical conclusion: among paadarivaar (பாடறிவார், 'those who know the nature or proper manner', from பாடு, 'way, condition'), panbu remains even within pagai (பகை, 'enmity'). Mu. Varadarasanar reads the paadarivaar as those who act knowing others' nature; Pappaiah expands that such people do not ridicule even foes; Pope renders 'Contempt is evil though in sport. They who man's nature know, / E'en in their wrath, a courteous mind will show.' The jingle nagaiyullum ... pagaiyullum binds jest and enmity as the two tests of courtesy. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita defines the discipline of speech as words that are true and pleasant and that do not disturb others' minds.
hinduism.tie_back: Speech that never agitates another rules out the hurtful jest the Kural warns against.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 17.15 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; good on non-wounding speech, but it does not address jesting or enemies specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: “As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs compares the one who harms a neighbour and then says he was only joking to a madman throwing deadly arrows.
christianity.tie_back: This is a near one-to-one match for the Kural's warning that ridicule wounds even in jest.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; an exact parallel on harm hidden in 'sport', though it does not extend to courtesy toward enemies.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, let not a people ridicule [another] people; perhaps they may be better than them; nor let women ridicule [other] women; perhaps they may be better than them. And do not insult one another and do not call each other by [offensive] nicknames.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an forbids mocking, insulting and name-calling, reminding the mocker that the mocked may be better than he.
islam.tie_back: It directly forbids the ridicule that the Kural says hurts even when meant as fun.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on the prohibition of ridicule.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Anyone who humiliates another in public, it is as though he were spilling blood.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud teaches that shaming someone so that the blood drains from his face is comparable to bloodshed.
judaism.tie_back: The rabbis, like Valluvar, treat the wound of contempt as real injury, not a harmless matter.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 58b (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong on the harm of humiliation, without the Kural's jest-and-enemy framing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak not harshly to anyone, for those thus spoken to might retort. Indeed, angry speech hurts, and retaliation may overtake you.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that harsh speech wounds others and breeds retaliation.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's insight that wounding words, toward anyone at all, cause real pain.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 133 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good on hurtful speech, though it does not mention jest.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He should not tell anything sinful or meaningless or hurtful, neither for his own sake nor for anybody else's, nor without such a motive.”
jainism.explanation: The lecture on discipline forbids hurtful speech for any reason, including speech with no motive at all.
jainism.tie_back: Ruling out hurtful words even 'without a motive' covers the idle or joking ridicule the Kural condemns.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable match on hurtful speech, though jest and enemies are not named.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Thersites jeers at Agamemnon to make the Greek soldiers laugh, and Odysseus beats him with the sceptre while the army laughs at him in turn.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer's portrait of Thersites shows mockery used for laughter that ends in humiliation and pain.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode illustrates the Kural's warning that ridicule, even when aimed at a laugh, wounds and breeds hostility.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not re-verified this session; an illustrative episode rather than a teaching on courtesy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Those who carry humour to excess are thought to be vulgar buffoons, striving after humour at all costs, and aiming rather at raising a laugh than at saying what is becoming and at avoiding pain to the object of their fun.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle condemns the buffoon whose jokes ignore the pain they cause their target, and praises tactful wit.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle names exactly the Kural's concern: a joke that wounds its object is a failure of good character.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.8 (tr. W. D. Ross, Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a near one-to-one match on jesting that pains its target.

kurals.tamil:
பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம் அதுஇன்றேல்
மண்புக்கு மாய்வது மன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Panputaiyaarp pattuntu ulakam adhuindrel
manpukku maaivadhu man.
kurals.meaning: The world keeps going because it rests on people of courteous character; without them it would sink into the earth and perish.
kurals.elementary: A tent stands up because of its poles. Take the poles away and the whole tent falls flat on the ground. Valluvar says kind, well-mannered people are the poles that hold up the whole world.
kurals.university: Ulagam (உலகம்) here means the ongoing life of human society; it 'exists' (undu, உண்டு) because it is pattu (பட்டு, 'resting upon, attached to') the panbudaiyaar (பண்புடையார், 'people of character'). Without that support it would man-pukku maaivadhu (மண்புக்கு மாய்வது), 'enter the earth and perish', the final man (மன்) being an emphatic particle. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses pattu as 'by being joined to' the courteous; Kalaignar reads ulagam as 'the conduct of the world'; Pope's prose 'The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good' follows the traditional line. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes the second line very differently, as 'even supplication would be meaningless', which departs from the classical gloss of man-pukku as 'entering the soil'. The kural echoes kural 571 on kannottam, where the world exists through the gracious. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “If I did not perform prescribed duties, all these worlds would be put to ruination. I would be the cause of creating unwanted population, and I would thereby destroy the peace of all living beings.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna says that if he ceased to act rightly as an example, the worlds would fall into ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ties the survival of the world to right conduct, though here the support is divine rather than courteous people.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 3.24 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; it shares the 'world would collapse' structure, but the sustaining agent is Krishna's dutiful action, not courteous humans.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And the LORD said, If I find in Sodom fifty righteous within the city, then I will spare all the place for their sakes.”
christianity.explanation: God tells Abraham that a city may be preserved from destruction for the sake of the righteous within it.
christianity.tie_back: The idea that the good keep a whole community from perishing is close to the Kural's image of the world resting on the courteous.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong match on the righteous sustaining a society, framed as divine mercy.

islam.quote_or_event: “And if it were not for Allah checking [some] people by means of others, the earth would have been corrupted, but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an teaches that God uses some people to restrain others, and that without this the earth would be ruined.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that the world is kept from ruin through the action of good people.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; it shares the 'earth would be ruined' motif, but the context is the restraint of evil, not courtesy.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Shimon the Righteous was one of the last of the men of the great assembly. He used to say: the world stands upon three things: the Torah, the Temple service, and the practice of acts of piety.”
judaism.explanation: One of the founding sayings of rabbinic ethics names acts of loving-kindness (gemilut hasadim) as one of the pillars on which the world stands.
judaism.tie_back: The image of the world 'standing upon' kindly conduct is the same as the Kural's world resting on people of good character.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 1:2 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong structural match, though two of the three pillars are religious rather than social.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Generosity, sweet speech, / Helpfulness to others, / Impartiality to all, / As the case demands. / These four winning ways make the world go round, / As the linchpin in a moving car.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha's four bases of social harmony (sangaha-vatthu), generosity, kind speech, helpfulness and impartiality, are said to keep the world turning like a linchpin.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural's claim: courtesy and kindness are what hold the world together.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (tr. Narada Thera, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match, with courteous virtues explicitly called the linchpin of the world.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The most excellent twice-born men who possess these good qualities, are able to save themselves and others.”
jainism.explanation: Gayaghosha concludes that those who truly possess the virtues he has described can rescue not only themselves but others too.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain text, like the Kural, sees people of real virtue as the ones on whom others' welfare depends.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 25.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match, as it concerns spiritual rescue rather than the survival of the social world.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And then Aidos and Nemesis, with their sweet forms wrapped in white robes, will go from the wide-pathed earth and forsake mankind to join the company of the deathless gods: and bitter sorrows will be left for mortal men, and there will be no help against evil.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod foresees that when the goddesses of shame and righteous indignation abandon humanity, nothing will remain to protect people from ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, Hesiod imagines a world that collapses once decency and right feeling depart.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 197–201 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White; sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match on the world's ruin without decency, personified as goddesses.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Zeus feared that the entire race would be exterminated, and so he sent Hermes to them, bearing reverence and justice to be the ordering principles of cities and the bonds of friendship and conciliation.”
philosophy.explanation: In Protagoras' myth, humans gathered in cities begin to destroy each other until Zeus gives them reverence and justice as the bonds of social life.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis in mythic form: without the qualities of refined character, human society would perish.
philosophy.source: Plato, Protagoras 322c (tr. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a close conceptual match on society surviving only through shared moral qualities.

kurals.tamil:
அரம்போலும் கூர்மைய ரேனும் மரம்போல்வர்
மக்கட்பண்பு இல்லா தவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Arampolum koormaiya renum marampolvar
makkatpanpu illaa thavar.
kurals.meaning: Those without humane qualities are no better than trees, even if their minds are as sharp as a file.
kurals.elementary: A pencil sharpener is very sharp, but it can't give you a hug or say sorry. Valluvar says a person can be super clever, but if they aren't kind they are like a tree trunk: standing there, but not really acting like a person.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on the rhyme aram (அரம், 'file, rasp') and maram (மரம், 'tree'): those who lack makkat-panbu (மக்கட்பண்பு, 'the quality proper to human beings') are 'like trees' even if they have a file's koormai (கூர்மை, 'sharpness'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss maram as ஓரறிவுயிர், 'a one-sensed being', invoking the classical Tamil (and Jain) grading of living beings by the number of their senses, so the insult is precise: an intellect without humanity sinks to the lowest rung of life. Pope renders 'Though sharp their wit as file, as blocks they must remain, / Whose souls are void of courtesy humane'. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads aram as a sharp cutting tool and makkat-panbu as 'humanitarianism'. The kural extends the argument of 993 from likeness to humanity itself. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: A well-known verse in the introduction to the Hitopadesha says that eating, sleeping, fear and mating are common to humans and animals; dharma alone is what sets humans apart, and those lacking it are equal to beasts.
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit fable collection teaches that what makes a human being more than an animal is moral character, not bodily functions or cleverness.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a person without the qualities proper to humans is reduced to a lower form of life.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely cited verse, not re-verified against a specific translation this session; the thought closely matches the Kural.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And though I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries, and all knowledge; and though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing.”
christianity.explanation: Paul says that even the greatest knowledge and gifts count for nothing without love.
christianity.tie_back: A mind sharp enough to know all mysteries but empty of love is the Kural's sharp file that is still only a tree.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on intellect without love being worthless.

islam.quote_or_event: “The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books].”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an likens those who carry knowledge without living by it to a donkey loaded with books.
islam.tie_back: The image of a beast carrying learning it does not embody parallels the Kural's sharp-witted person who is still like a tree.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a good match on knowledge without character reducing one to a lower creature.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He used to say: one whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what may he be compared? To a tree whose branches are numerous but whose roots are few, so that when the wind comes, it uproots it and overturns it.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah compares the person whose learning outstrips his conduct to a tree that topples in the wind.
judaism.tie_back: By a striking coincidence of imagery, it too likens wisdom without goodness to a tree.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 3:17 (Mishnah Yomit, tr. Joshua Kulp, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; strong match on wisdom outstripping deeds, with a shared tree image used to a slightly different end.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Much though he recites the sacred texts, but acts not accordingly, that heedless man is like a cowherd who only counts the cows of others — he does not partake of the blessings of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that learning recited but not lived brings no real benefit.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats knowledge cut off from good conduct as empty.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 19 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good on learning without practice, though it does not speak of humaneness.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Acknowledging the truth about bondage and liberation, but talking only, not acting (in accordance with these tenets), they seek comfort for themselves in mighty words. Clever talking will not work salvation; how should philosophical instruction do it? Fools, though sinking lower and lower through their sins, believe themselves to be wise men.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira rejects those who rely on clever talk and doctrine while failing to act rightly, calling them fools who think themselves wise.
jainism.tie_back: This matches the Kural's sharp-minded person who lacks the conduct that makes one truly human.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 6.9–10 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit on cleverness without conduct; the Kural's 'one-sensed tree' image also echoes the Jain grading of beings by senses.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Homer describes the Cyclopes as lawless and overbearing beings who hold no assemblies and have no laws, each ruling his own family without regard for others; Polyphemus later scorns the guest-right of Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Cyclopes are powerful and capable, yet lack the social and moral qualities of civilized humans.
greek_mythology.tie_back: They embody the Kural's being who has capacity but lacks the qualities that make one fully human.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not re-verified this session; a reasonable illustration, though Polyphemus is not portrayed as especially sharp-witted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but, when separated from law and justice, he is the worst of all; since armed injustice is the more dangerous, and he is equipped at birth with arms, meant to be used by intelligence and virtue, which he may use for the worst ends.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that human intelligence without virtue makes man not the best but the worst and most savage of animals.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, Aristotle says that a sharp intellect without humane virtue sinks a person below the human.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Politics I.2, 1253a (tr. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a strong conceptual match on intelligence without virtue.

kurals.tamil:
நண்பாற்றார் ஆகி நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்
பண்பாற்றார் ஆதல் கடை.
kurals.transliteration:
Nanpaatraar aaki nayamila seyvaarkkum
panpaatraar aadhal katai.
kurals.meaning: Failing to be courteous, even toward those who are unfriendly and do us wrong, is the lowest disgrace.
kurals.elementary: If a classmate keeps being mean to you, it is tempting to be mean back. But Valluvar says the really strong thing is to stay polite anyway. Being rude back would make you lose something precious of your own.
kurals.university: The couplet carries the chapter's ethic to its hardest case. Nanb-aatraar (நண்பாற்றார்) are those who 'do not practise friendship', and nayam-ila seyvaar (நயமில செய்வார்) those who 'do unpleasant, unjust things'; even toward them, to be panb-aatraar (பண்பாற்றார், 'not practising courtesy') is kadai (கடை), 'the lowest, the worst'. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as a disgrace (இழிவு) to abandon courtesy in the face of hostility; Kalaignar adds patience (பொறுமை) as the means. Pope's 'Though men with all unfriendly acts and wrongs assail, / 'Tis uttermost disgrace in courtesy to fail' captures the parallel of nanbaatraar ... panbaatraar. The kural echoes kural 314 on 'shaming' wrongdoers by doing them good. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is equal to friends and enemies, who is equipoised in honor and dishonor, heat and cold, happiness and distress, fame and infamy, who is always free from contaminating association, always silent and satisfied with anything, who doesn’t care for any residence, who is fixed in knowledge and who is engaged in devotional service – such a person is very dear to Me.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna praises the devotee who treats friend and enemy alike and stays steady under insult.
hinduism.tie_back: Even-mindedness toward enemies parallels the Kural's demand to keep courtesy toward the hostile.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 12.18–19 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; good on equal treatment of enemies, but it stresses inner equanimity rather than active courtesy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I say unto you which hear, Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus commands active goodwill toward enemies and those who mistreat us.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural's teaching in its strongest form: answer hostility with goodness, not rudeness.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match, going even beyond courtesy to love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an instructs believers to answer evil with something better, promising that enmity may turn into friendship.
islam.tie_back: Answering the unfriendly with good conduct is exactly what the Kural asks.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a near one-to-one match on meeting hostility with better conduct.

judaism.quote_or_event: “If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the LORD shall reward thee.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs commands kindness to an enemy in need, promising divine reward.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it requires generous, decent conduct toward those who are hostile.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong match on goodness toward enemies, with a note of moral pressure in the 'coals of fire'.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By non-hatred alone is hatred appeased. This is a law eternal.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that only non-hatred, not retaliation, can end enmity.
buddhism.tie_back: Refusing to return hostility for hostility is the inner basis of the Kural's courtesy toward the unfriendly.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 5 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong thematic match, though it speaks of hatred rather than outward courtesy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If a layman abuses a monk, he should not grow angry against him; because he would be like a child, a monk should not grow angry. If a monk hears bad words, cruel and rankling ones, he should silently overlook them, and not take them to heart.”
jainism.explanation: Among the twenty-two hardships a monk must bear is abuse (akrosa), which he must meet without anger, overlooking cruel words.
jainism.tie_back: This Jain discipline of bearing abuse without retaliation closely matches the Kural's refusal to abandon courtesy toward the hostile.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.24–25 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong match on non-retaliation, framed as monastic endurance.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Returning home disguised as a beggar, Odysseus endures insults, kicks and thrown stools from the goatherd Melanthius and the suitors in his own hall, holding back his anger until the time for vengeance.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus shows great restraint under abuse, though his patience is strategic and ends in slaughter.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His restraint resembles the Kural's composure before the hostile, but his aim is revenge rather than courtesy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory; a next-best match only, since Odysseus' restraint serves eventual vengeance.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then we ought not to retaliate or render evil for evil to anyone, whatever evil we may have suffered from him.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates, awaiting execution, insists that no wrong, however grave, justifies doing wrong in return.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the philosophical core of the Kural's teaching that courtesy must hold even toward those who wrong us.
philosophy.source: Plato, Crito 49c (tr. Benjamin Jowett, Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a strong match on non-retaliation, though Socrates speaks of injury rather than manners.

kurals.tamil:
நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு மாயிரு ஞாலம்
பகலும்பாற் பட்டன்று இருள்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nakalvallar allaarkku maayiru gnaalam
pakalumpaar pattandru irul.
kurals.meaning: For those who cannot share in friendly, cheerful company, this vast wide world lies in darkness even in broad daylight.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a sunny day at the park, but you won't play, laugh, or talk with anyone. Even with the sun shining, it would feel gloomy. Valluvar says a heart that can't smile and join in makes the whole world feel dark.
kurals.university: Nagal vallar allaar (நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்) are 'those not able to laugh', that is, unable to mix with others and share friendly cheer; for them maa-iru gnaalam (மாயிரு ஞாலம், 'the great, vast earth') is, even by day (pagalum), fallen into darkness (paal patta-andru irul, பாற்பட்டன்று இருள்). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses nagal as 'mingling with others and rejoicing' (பிறரோடு கலந்து பழகி மகிழ), Pappaiah ties it explicitly to lack of good character, and Kalaignar to inability to enjoy friends; Pope's prose 'To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light' follows this line. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads nagal as 'harmonizing with others' and iru as 'two-fold', an idiosyncratic segmentation. The transliteration of gnaalam varies across sites (Gnaalam on ytamizh, ñālam on thirukkural.net). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “One who is not connected with the Supreme [in Kṛṣṇa consciousness] can have neither transcendental intelligence nor a steady mind, without which there is no possibility of peace. And how can there be any happiness without peace?”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that without an inner connection there is no peace, and without peace no happiness.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts say that the lack of an inner quality turns life joyless, though the Gita's missing quality is spiritual connection rather than sociable cheer.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.66 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; a next-best match only, as it concerns spiritual peace rather than friendly cheerfulness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.”
christianity.explanation: Proverbs contrasts the gloom of the downcast with the cheerful heart that makes every day a feast.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says the inner capacity for cheer colours the whole world, turning days to gloom or feast.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; good match on cheerfulness shaping one's whole experience, without the social element.

islam.quote_or_event: “Your smiling in the face of your brother is charity, commanding good and forbidding evil is charity, your giving directions to a man lost in the land is charity for you.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet counts a smile offered to another as an act of charity.
islam.tie_back: It shares the Kural's high regard for warm, smiling sociability as a moral good.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a reasonable match on the value of a cheerful face, though it does not describe the gloom of its absence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “They said to him: We are jesters, and we cheer up the depressed. Alternatively, when we see two people who have a quarrel between them, we strive to make peace.”
judaism.explanation: Elijah points out two jesters in the marketplace as destined for the World to Come because they bring cheer to the sad and make peace.
judaism.tie_back: The Talmud prizes the very capacity for shared laughter that the Kural says keeps the world from darkness.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Taanit 22a (William Davidson Edition, Koren-Steinsaltz English, via Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong match on the moral worth of cheerful sociability, from the positive side.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Dhammapada the Buddha's disciples declare that they live happily, possessing nothing, and will feed on joy like the Radiant Gods.
buddhism.explanation: The verse celebrates a joy (piti) that does not depend on possessions.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural's sense that joy lights up life, though Buddhist joy is inward and ascetic rather than social.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, as the page could not be re-fetched this session; a next-best match, since its joy is renunciant rather than sociable.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Though emaciated like the joint of a crow's (leg) and covered with a network of veins, he should know the permitted measure of food and drink, and wander about with a cheerful mind.”
jainism.explanation: Even when worn thin by fasting, the Jain monk is told to go about with a cheerful mind.
jainism.tie_back: The Jain stress on cheerfulness in all conditions touches the Kural's point that a joyless mind darkens life, though without its social dimension.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 2.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a next-best match, since the cheerfulness is ascetic endurance rather than friendly laughter.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “A long time she sat upon the stool without speaking because of her sorrow, and greeted no one by word or by sign, but rested, never smiling, and tasting neither food nor drinks because she pined with longing for her deep-bosomed daughter, until careful Iambe -- who pleased her moods in aftertime also -- moved the holy lady with many a quip and jest to smile and laugh and cheer her heart.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The grieving Demeter, who has withdrawn from all company, is drawn back into life by Iambe's jokes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Demeter's unsmiling isolation and the light that returns with laughter dramatize the Kural's image of a world dark without shared cheer.
greek_mythology.source: Homeric Hymn 2, To Demeter 198–204 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White; sacred-texts.com)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a vivid narrative parallel to the darkness of a heart that cannot laugh.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “While those who can neither make a joke themselves nor put up with those who do are thought to be boorish and unpolished.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle calls the person who can neither joke nor bear joking boorish, lacking a social virtue needed for good company.
philosophy.tie_back: This is Aristotle's name for the Kural's nagal vallar allaar, those unable to share in laughter.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IV.8 (tr. W. D. Ross, Internet Classics Archive)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on classics.mit.edu; a close match on the person who cannot laugh, though without the image of darkness.

kurals.tamil:
பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம் நன்பால்
கலந்தீமை யால்திரிந் தற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Panpilaan petra perunjelvam nanpaal
kalandheemai yaaldhirin thatru.
kurals.meaning: Great wealth that comes to a person without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by an unclean vessel.
kurals.elementary: Pour fresh milk into a dirty cup and it turns sour and yucky. Valluvar says money is like that milk: if it goes to a rude, unkind person, it turns sour and does nobody any good.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a domestic simile: the perum-selvam (பெருஞ்செல்வம், 'great wealth') of the panbilaan (பண்பிலான், 'man without courtesy') is like nan-paal (நன்பால், 'good milk') that has 'turned' (thirindhu, திரிந்து) through kalam-theemai (கலந்தீமை, 'defect of the vessel'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read kalan as the container (கலம், பாத்திரம்), Kalaignar specifying a vessel coated with verdigris (களிம்பு); Pope's verse 'Like sweet milk soured because in filthy vessel poured' agrees, while his prose 'will perish like pure milk spoilt by the impurity of the vessel' stresses waste. The segmentation kalan + theemai, rather than kalandhu + theemai ('mixed with evil'), is the standard one; Sivayogi Sivakumar's 'by the evil mixed with it' reflects the alternative split. The kural also bridges to the next chapter, Nanriyil Selvam (ch. 101, 'Useless wealth'). Transliterations differ slightly (yaaldhirinh thatru on ytamizh; yaaldhirin thatru on thirukkural.net), but the Tamil text is identical on both sites.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The demoniac person thinks: “So much wealth do I have today, and I will gain more according to my schemes. So much is mine now, and it will increase in the future, more and more. He is my enemy, and I have killed him, and my other enemies will also be killed. I am the lord of everything. I am the enjoyer. I am perfect, powerful and happy. I am the richest man, surrounded by aristocratic relatives. There is none so powerful and happy as I am. I shall perform sacrifices, I shall give some charity, and thus I shall rejoice.” In this way, such persons are deluded by ignorance.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna depicts how wealth in the hands of a person of demonic character feeds arrogance, enmity and delusion.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows riches turning to evil in a person without good character.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 16.13–15 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on vedabase.io; good on wealth corrupted by bad character, without the Kural's image of spoiled goodness.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do men put new wine into old bottles: else the bottles break, and the wine runneth out, and the bottles perish: but they put new wine into new bottles, and both are preserved.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus' parable warns that a good substance poured into an unfit container is lost along with the container.
christianity.tie_back: It shares the Kural's image of a good thing ruined by an unfit vessel, though Jesus applies it to his new teaching.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a close image but a different application, so only a partial match.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury as does one who spends his wealth [only] to be seen by the people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is like that of a [large] smooth stone upon which is dust and is hit by a downpour that leaves it bare.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an warns that wealth given with insult or for show is washed away, leaving nothing of value.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows the good of wealth spoiled by the giver's ungracious character.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a reasonable match on wealth nullified by discourtesy, focused on charity.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There is a sore evil which I have seen under the sun, namely, riches kept for the owners thereof to their hurt.”
judaism.explanation: Ecclesiastes observes that wealth can be hoarded only to harm its owner.
judaism.tie_back: This shares the Kural's insight that riches can turn bad in the wrong hands.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a partial match on wealth gone sour, without naming character as the cause.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Riches ruin only the foolish, not those in quest of the Beyond. By craving for riches the witless man ruins himself as well as others.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada teaches that wealth destroys the foolish but not the wise.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, whether wealth is good or ruinous depends on the character of its holder.
buddhism.source: Dhammapada 355 (tr. Acharya Buddharakkhita, Access to Insight)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; a good match on wealth spoiled by the holder's flaws, with folly rather than discourtesy as the flaw.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Men who adhering to wrong principles acquire wealth by evil deeds, will lose it, falling into the snares (of their passions) and being held captive by their hatred.” … “Wealth will not protect a careless man in this world and the next. Though he had seen the right way, he does not see it, even as one in the dark whose lamp has suddenly been put out.”
jainism.explanation: Mahavira teaches that wealth gained or held without right conduct is lost and brings no protection.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it shows wealth becoming useless and ruinous when held by one lacking good character.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 4.2 and 4.5 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a reasonable match on wealth failing the morally careless, though not about courtesy specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Granted his wish that everything he touched would turn to gold, King Midas finds that his food and drink become metal in his mouth, so that his great wealth becomes a curse until he begs to be released from it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas' foolish greed turns the gift of riches into something that cannot nourish him.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like milk spoiled in a bad vessel, wealth in the hands of the unwise turns from blessing to curse.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not re-verified this session; it shares the theme of wealth spoiled by its holder, though Midas' flaw is greed rather than discourtesy.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Sincerum est nisi uas, quodcumque infundis acescit.”
philosophy.explanation: Horace tells Lollius that unless the vessel is clean, whatever you pour into it turns sour, meaning that possessions and pleasures cannot benefit a corrupted mind.
philosophy.tie_back: Horace uses the very same image as the Kural, a good liquid spoiled by an impure vessel, to say that wealth is wasted on a flawed character.
philosophy.source: Horace, Epistles 1.2.54 (Latin text, The Latin Library)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in Latin on thelatinlibrary.com (English gloss is my own); a near one-to-one match in both image and meaning.
